description: Despite the name and the loss of our actual astrophobic member, the astrophobics are enthusiasts of both space and earth science, looking to hone our computer science and graphic design skills in fun ways such as a hackathon!
summary:
AstroBox is an interactive web platform that turns real NASA Earth science data into real-time, procedurally generated soundscapes. Users explore a 3D globe and 2D map, moving a companion character, Verny, to different locations to hear how those places sound. Rainfall intensity, wind, climate zones, and nearby wildfires shape the audio, which is generated directly in the browser with the Web Audio API rather than from prerecorded files. Guided stories, such as El Niño and the orographic rain shadow effect in northern Mexico, combine sound, maps, and visual effects to explain complex phenomena.

AstroBox answers NASA’s challenge of translating visual Earth science into sound by using NASA POWER, EONET, and GIBS data, along with Open-Meteo and Esri’s Köppen-Geiger climate data. Sound here represents the behavior of the data itself, not decoration.

It matters because it makes Earth science more accessible and engaging for people with visual impairments, children, and non-scientific audiences. Keyboard navigation, screen-reader-friendly panels, and user-controlled sound categories support inclusive use. Our vision: NASA gives us the eyes to see our planet, and AstroBox gives it a voice.
details:
AstroBox

AstroBox is an interactive web platform that transforms real Earth science data into dynamic, real-time soundscapes, allowing people to explore and understand our changing planet through sound.

Inspired by NASA's challenge to translate visual Earth science into sound, AstroBox introduces a new way to experience environmental information. Instead of relying exclusively on maps and satellite imagery, our platform gives scientific data an auditory dimension.

Users can explore Earth through an interactive 3D globe and 2D map. By moving our companion character, Verny, to different geographical locations, users can discover how those places sound based on their environmental conditions.

For example, precipitation data determines the intensity of rainfall sounds: heavier rainfall produces more intense sounds, while lower precipitation generates softer rainfall. Wind conditions influence gusts and whistles, while climate zones and nearby fire events contribute to different environmental soundscapes.

The experience is enhanced by synchronized visual effects and guided storytelling experiences that help users understand complex phenomena such as El Niño and the orographic rain shadow effect in northern Mexico.

Benefits and Key Features

AstroBox offers several benefits:

  • Accessibility: Provides an alternative way to experience scientific information through sound, particularly for people with visual impairments and users who may find traditional scientific visualizations difficult to interpret.
  • Interactive learning: Makes Earth science more engaging for children, teenagers, and non-scientific audiences.
  • Real-time procedural sonification: Generates sounds dynamically from environmental data rather than relying on prerecorded audio files. Each location and environmental condition can produce a different auditory experience.
  • Multisensory exploration: Combines sound, satellite imagery, maps, animations, and interactive visual effects.
  • Guided scientific storytelling: Transforms complex environmental processes into structured, easy-to-follow auditory and visual journeys.
  • User control: Allows users to activate or deactivate sound categories, navigate using a keyboard, and access information through panels designed to support screen readers.

Intended Impact

Our main goal is to make Earth science more accessible, inclusive, and engaging.

We want children to discover the planet through sound, teenagers to develop a better understanding of climate phenomena, and people with visual impairments to access environmental information through an additional sensory channel.

AstroBox promotes environmental awareness by helping users connect scientific data with real-world phenomena. By experiencing changes in rainfall, wind, temperature, and other environmental conditions, users can develop a more intuitive understanding of how interconnected our planet is.

Our long-term vision is to expand AstroBox into an educational and accessibility platform for science museums, classrooms, planetariums, and institutions such as NASA's Earth Information Center. We envision a system where new NASA visualizations can be paired with their own auditory experiences.

Technologies and Tools Used

AstroBox was developed using web technologies and open scientific data services.

Programming languages and frameworks:

  • Angular 22: Main application framework, component architecture, state management, and server-side rendering.
  • TypeScript: Application logic and data processing.
  • HTML and CSS: Interface structure, styling, and visual effects.
  • JavaScript Web APIs: Native browser capabilities for audio generation and visual rendering.

Scientific data sources and APIs:

  • NASA POWER: Environmental data including precipitation, temperature, and wind conditions.
  • NASA EONET v3: Natural event information, including wildfire events.
  • NASA GIBS: Satellite imagery and Earth observation layers, including precipitation and sea surface temperature.
  • Open-Meteo: Global wind data for animated wind patterns.
  • Esri ArcGIS Köppen-Geiger: Global climate classification data.
  • Esri World Street Map: Geographic map information.

Libraries and technologies:

  • CesiumJS: Interactive 3D globe, 2D map, geographic layers, and story animations.
  • Web Audio API: Procedural sound generation using oscillators, noise generators, and audio filters.
  • Canvas 2D: Rain, fire, wind, and other visual effects.
  • LERC / WebAssembly: Decoding climate classification raster tiles.
  • Express: Server-side application support.
  • RxJS: Managing guided story events and sequences.

Creativity and Innovation

AstroBox's main creative innovation is treating sound as a language for communicating scientific data.

Rather than simply adding audio to an existing visualization, we developed a procedural sound engine that translates environmental variables into dynamic auditory experiences.

This means that sound is not decorative: it represents the behavior of the data itself.

Another innovative element is Verny, our interactive companion. Users can move Verny across the planet and discover how different geographical locations produce different soundscapes.

We also introduced guided stories that combine scientific information, sound, maps, and visual effects to explain complex phenomena in an accessible and engaging way.

Our approach brings together environmental science, procedural audio, interactive geography, and inclusive design in a single web experience.

Factors Considered During Development

Our team considered several important factors:

  1. Scientific reliability: We prioritized public scientific data sources and distinguish observed data from illustrative effects.
  2. Accessibility: We considered keyboard navigation, screen-reader-compatible information panels, and auditory alternatives to visual information.
  3. Real-time performance: We designed the sound engine to generate audio directly in the browser without requiring prerecorded sound files.
  4. Scalability: We structured the platform so additional environmental datasets, sound categories, and guided stories can be incorporated without rebuilding the entire application.
  5. User experience: We designed Verny and the guided stories to make complex scientific information easier to explore and understand.
  6. Web accessibility: We chose browser-based technologies so users can access the experience without installing specialized software.

Our vision is simple: NASA gives us the eyes to see our planet. AstroBox gives it a voice.

We believe understanding how Earth changes should not depend on how a person perceives the world. If we can hear it, we can begin to understand it.
